summary: Specifies three sets of new ciphersuites for TLS that authenticate using pre-shared keys. The first uses only symmetric operations, the second adds a Diffie-Hellman exchange authenticated with the key, and the third combines public key authentication of the server with pre-shared key authentication of the client. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4279 adds TLS ciphersuites that authenticate with a secret the parties already share. It defines three families, which differ in whether they use only that secret, add Diffie-Hellman, or also authenticate the server with RSA.

does tls psk provide forward secrecy
subtitle: Three TLS ciphersuite families that use a key the parties share in advance.

tldr.problem: TLS commonly authenticates with certificates or Kerberos. Some limited or closed environments may prefer a shared secret that is easier to configure or avoids some public-key operations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4279 defines PSK, DHE_PSK and RSA_PSK ciphersuite families. The client identifies the pre-shared key, and the handshake combines it with zeroes, a Diffie-Hellman result or an RSA-encrypted value.
tldr.outcome: The families provide different trade-offs in public-key use and forward secrecy. RFC 4279 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 10015.

today: RFC 4279 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 10015. Consult those updates for changes that apply to the ciphersuites described here.

sections.title: When TLS Uses a Shared Secret
sections.content:
A pre-shared key (PSK) is a symmetric key shared by the communicating parties before a TLS connection. RFC 4279 defines TLS ciphersuites that use PSKs for authentication.

The RFC identifies two possible advantages: some ciphersuites avoid public-key operations, and manual configuration of a shared key may suit a closed environment. It says the ciphersuites target a limited set of applications, usually with few clients and servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The parties configure the same secret before connecting. TLS can use that secret to authenticate the connection instead of relying only on certificates.

sections.title: The PSK Handshake
sections.content:
The client lists PSK ciphersuites in its ClientHello, and the server selects one in its ServerHello. The normal certificate messages are omitted for this method. The client sends a PSK identity in ClientKeyExchange so the server can select the matching key.

The client and server combine the PSK with a same-length string of zeroes to form the premaster secret. The handshake is then authenticated using the usual TLS Finished messages. If the server does not recognize the identity, it may send an unknown_psk_identity alert or respond as if the key were wrong.
sections.plainLanguage: The client names the shared key it intends to use. Both sides build the same TLS secret from that key and confirm the handshake.

sections.title: DHE_PSK Adds a Fresh Key Exchange
sections.content:
The DHE_PSK family combines a PSK with a Diffie-Hellman exchange. The server sends its Diffie-Hellman parameters, and the client sends its public value together with the PSK identity. Both sides include the Diffie-Hellman result and the PSK in the premaster secret.

The RFC says DHE_PSK provides protection against dictionary attacks by passive eavesdroppers and provides perfect forward secrecy when the server generates a fresh Diffie-Hellman private key for each handshake. Passive listening alone does not give an attacker the information needed for the described offline attack.
sections.plainLanguage: DHE_PSK creates a fresh shared value and uses the PSK to authenticate the exchange. With a fresh private value for each handshake, it provides perfect forward secrecy.

sections.title: RSA_PSK Uses a Server Certificate
sections.content:
The RSA_PSK family authenticates the server with RSA and a certificate, while also using the PSK. The server sends a Certificate message. The client sends its PSK identity and an encrypted premaster secret containing a version number and random value.

The premaster secret combines that version and random value with the PSK. The RFC does not define what else the certificate contains or how it is validated. RSA_PSK does not provide perfect forward secrecy.
sections.plainLanguage: RSA_PSK uses both a server certificate and a shared secret. The client sends a value encrypted for the server, and the PSK is also part of the resulting secret.

sections.title: Identity Encoding and Implementation Limits
sections.content:
The PSK identity is first treated as a character string and then encoded as UTF-8. The RFC does not require one specific identity type. Unless an application profile says otherwise, a server should not send an identity hint, and a client must ignore one.

TLS implementations must support PSK identities up to 128 octets and PSKs up to 64 octets; support for longer values is recommended. Management interfaces have corresponding requirements for entering identities and keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server must encode a PSK identity in the same way. Implementations must support identities up to 128 octets and keys up to 64 octets.

sections.title: Ciphersuites and Security Risks
sections.content:
The RFC defines twelve ciphersuites across the three families and the unknown_psk_identity alert. A short or human-chosen PSK can be vulnerable to brute-force or dictionary attacks. The RFC recommends that interfaces that allow manual PSK entry also offer a way to generate a random key.

The PSK identity is sent in cleartext and can reveal who is communicating. Plain PSK and RSA_PSK do not provide perfect forward secrecy; DHE_PSK can provide it with a fresh Diffie-Hellman private key for each handshake. The RFC notes that captured handshakes expose different levels of information for offline attacks in each family.
sections.plainLanguage: A weak shared secret can be guessed, and the identity is visible to observers. Only DHE_PSK can provide perfect forward secrecy, and it needs a fresh Diffie-Hellman private value each time.
